opening.headline: After changing the model, to prevent a sharp decline in quality among some customers, you learn the model transition process consisting of evaluation, staged deployment, and rollback.
body: When a new model is released, you may wish to replace it hoping for better results. However, if you switch all traffic at once simply because average metrics are similar, you may experience a sudden drop in quality among certain customer segments. Since each model has different default behaviors and supported configurations, the same prompt does not necessarily yield the same results.

In this class, we divide model transitions into three elements: evaluation gates, staged deployments, and rollbacks. We then distinguish the risks at each transition stage, and through case studies that follow the rationale for gradually deploying models that have passed evaluation, we practice assessing the regression risks in transition plans.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the model transition procedure
The transition stage-specific risks can be distinguished.
Can assess the regression risk of the transition plan

screens.title: After changing the model, quality dropped in some customer segments.
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare the same transition results when viewed as a whole average versus when viewed by customer segment.

visual.alt: The overall average is similar, but when viewed by customer segment, one segment shows a significant drop in quality, as illustrated by the bar chart.

states.label: View by overall average
states.body:
The average metrics post-transition are similar to those before the transition. The error rate has not significantly increased, and responses to a few verification questions are satisfactory. Based solely on this screen, the transition appears successful, and the team decides to migrate all remaining traffic to the new model.

However, averages combine results from many customer segments into a single number. If most customer segments perform well, performance declines in a few segments may not be visible within the average.

states.label: View by customer segment
states.body:
When broken down by customer segment, it becomes clear that only enterprises in the group that submit lengthy documents experienced a decline in quality. Once the transition has been completed for all customers, the impact immediately spreads to all affected customers.

This happens because each model has different default behaviors and supported settings. The Claude migration documentation lists cases where settings such as thinking configuration, filled-in responses, and sampling parameters can go wrong depending on the model. The same prompt and settings do not guarantee identical results with a new model.

screens.outro: The question of this lesson is how to distribute risk across transition stages. First, let's recall the current verification procedures we are undertaking.

screens.title: Think back to the verification procedures when replacing a model.
screens.lead: First, think carefully about the question on your own and then choose. No content is entered or submitted; instead, what appears is the instructor's summary of thoughts.

items.prompt: Before replacing, is there any review item to consider?
items.answer: If there are evaluation criteria, we can objectively verify whether the new model exceeds the benchmark. If there are no criteria, judgment will be based solely on personal experience. The evaluation set developed in evaluation-based development becomes the first threshold for transition.

items.prompt: Should we switch all at once, or should we first send only a portion of the traffic to the new model?
items.answer: If all components are changed at once, all customers are affected when problems occur. If only a subset is rolled out first, the number of customers impacted in case of issues is limited. This difference significantly influences transition risk.

items.prompt: Can we roll back to a previous model if problems arise?
items.answer: Rollback options are too late to create after a problem occurs. By preserving the previous model ID, prompt, and settings together, and by pre-configuring a switch to toggle between them, recovery time is significantly reduced.

screens.outro: Now, let's examine the transition procedure involving evaluation, phased deployment, and rollback.

screens.title: Evaluation, staged deployment, rollback flowchart
screens.lead: Select the number marker to view the items to check at each step in the flowchart. Check them one by one from number 1.

visual.alt: Flow diagram for evaluation gate, phased deployment, observability, followed by scaling out or rollback.

markers.label: Change Review Check
markers.title: Verify changed behaviors by model
markers.body: Before migration, read the migration documentation for the new model and create a list of changed default behaviors and settings that cause errors. The Claude Sonnet 5.5 documentation indicates that five settings—thought budget, sampling parameters, filled responses, forced tool selection, and thinking deactivation—can result in error 400. Additionally, omitting the thinking setting causes adaptive thinking to be enabled by default, which is different from the previous model.

markers.label: evaluation gate
markers.title: You must exceed the evaluation set criteria to proceed to the next stage.
markers.body: Once the evaluation set meets the release criteria, proceed to the next stage. Continuously evaluate the development process based on evaluation criteria, and apply the same evaluation approach during model transitions. If the criteria are not met, adjust the prompt and re-evaluate. The Claude retirement document also recommends thoroughly testing the replacement model well in advance of the retirement date.

markers.label: Some traffic distribution
markers.title: Staged Deployment
markers.body: Even if evaluation is passed, it does not immediately switch to full deployment; instead, it sends the new model only to a portion of traffic, while maintaining the existing model for the rest. This is because the types missed in the evaluation set might actually appear in real traffic. Starting with a small scale ensures that, even if issues arise, only a limited number of customers are affected.

markers.label: Indicator observation
markers.title: Actual metric comparison between the two models
markers.body: Compares real-world metrics such as error rate, user feedback, and response length between the existing model and the new model. Do not look only at averages—break them down by customer segment. The Operations Excellence lens from Google Well-Architected principles emphasizes observability and automation throughout the model development lifecycle.

markers.label: Rollback
markers.title: Path to revert to previous model
markers.body: If an issue is detected, immediately roll back to the previous model. The rollback path must be prepared before the transition. Since the Claude model ID points to a fixed snapshot, you only need to preserve the previous ID along with its corresponding prompt and settings to enable easy rollback. Without a rollback path, recovery becomes longer and more complex.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the flow, let's categorize the risks hidden within each step in a table.

screens.title: Transition stage risks and prompt reconfiguration
screens.lead: The following table summarizes the risks that may occur at each transition stage and the corresponding mitigations. Follow the stages from top to bottom to verify which risks are reduced by which device.

data.notes: Risks vary by stage. It is not possible to mitigate all risks through a single assessment, so organizations must have responses across four layers: inspection, evaluation, deployment, and operations. Some models also require data retention for 30 days, so services with retention requirements should include this item in their transition inspection.

screens.outro: Since we have distinguished between procedures and risks, let's take the example of gradually rolling out a model that has passed evaluation to illustrate why such a phased deployment is necessary.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Reasons for Gradual Deployment Even After Passing Evaluation
screens.lead: The instructor provides a step-by-step explanation of a case involving a transition to a new model. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. The evaluation set and metrics for the case are assumed for illustrative purposes.

steps.title: See case
steps.body: The new model has passed the release criteria of the evaluation set. However, the evaluation set contained very few enterprise customer types that submit lengthy documents. The team is considering whether they can immediately proceed with a full rollout, given that the model has passed evaluation. Let's address this question step by step.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify gate passage confirmation
steps.body: Verify whether the evaluation results have exceeded the release criteria. Passing means there are no issues within the types included in the evaluation set. It provides no information about types not included in the evaluation set. Therefore, gate passing is a signal that transition can begin, not a signal that transition should end.

steps.title: Stage 2: Perform a Small-Scale Deployment
steps.body: Send only a portion of the traffic to the new model while maintaining the existing model for the rest. Start with a ratio that has minimal impact even if issues arise. Divide the traffic so both models receive requests over the same period and of the same type to ensure a fair comparison.

steps.title: Step 3: Observe the Indicator
steps.body: Compare metrics such as error rate, user feedback, and response length between two models. Look beyond just the average and break down by customer segment. The goal at this stage is to identify signals that were not present in the evaluation set.

steps.title: Step 4: Discover Regression
steps.body: The signal of poor response quality appears only among customers with long inputs. The issue, which was not visible in average metrics, becomes apparent when comparing customer segments. If the entire cohort had completed the conversion, the entire group would have been affected.

steps.title: Step 5: Perform Rollback
steps.body: This traffic is rolled back to the previous model to mitigate damage. Since the previous model ID, prompt, and settings were pre-archived, the rollback does not take a long time. Rollback is not a failure—it is the expected result of a small-scale deployment functioning as designed.

steps.title: Step 6: Evaluation Dataset and Prompt Enhancement
steps.body: Add the identified long input type to the evaluation set. Then, adjust the instructions and examples accordingly to match the behavior differences of the new model. Re-evaluate using the improved evaluation set and prompts to confirm whether the release criteria are exceeded.

steps.title: Step 7: Gradually increase the ratio
steps.body: If the criteria are met, the new model ratio is gradually increased. At each stage, the same metric is observed, and if issues are detected, the ratio is reverted. Even after reaching the final ratio, a path to revert back to the previous model is maintained for a certain period.

steps.title: Conclusion of the case
steps.body: The evaluation gate prevents known types of regressions, staged deployment and observability limit damage from regression types missed by the evaluation set, and rollback reduces recovery time after a discovery. Together, these three elements compensate for each other's weaknesses; if any one is missing, the risk of regression increases.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the benchmarks obtained from the case study.

screens.title: The transition consists of three elements: evaluation, gradualism, and rollback.
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson. Reflect on how to divide risks across transition stages, and read through it with that in mind.

paragraphs: Model switching consists of three elements: an evaluation gate that advances to the next stage only when predefined criteria are met, a staged deployment that begins with a portion of traffic and observes actual metrics, and rollback, which returns to the previous model when issues are detected.

Before the transition, review changed default behaviors and settings that cause errors in the migration documentation for the new model, and adjust the prompt accordingly for the new model. Each model has different default behaviors and supported settings, which is why the same prompt does not yield the same results.

Passing the evaluation applies only to the types contained within the evaluation set. Since the evaluation set does not capture all actual distributions, we pre-configure paths that start with a subset of traffic and observe and roll back by customer segment. When issues are detected, the affected type is added to the evaluation set, and the same regression is reprevented. This loop enhances the safety of transitions.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: When reviewing a transition plan, ask yourself three questions: Is there an evaluation gate? Does it start with some traffic? Is there a predefined rollback path? If any one of these is missing, the risk of regression increases accordingly.

glossary.def: This is a gateway requiring you to exceed predefined evaluation criteria in order to proceed to the next stage.
This is a method where we first apply a new model to a portion of traffic to observe metrics, and then gradually expand it.
It reverts to the previous model and configuration when a problem occurs.
This involves refining instructions and examples to align with the operational differences of the new model.
After the change, there is a possibility that previously working features may stop working properly.

misconceptions.myth: Once the evaluation is passed, you can switch at once.
misconceptions.fact: If there are types not covered by the evaluation set, the regression may go undetected even if the test passes. Actual metrics must be observed by starting with a subset of traffic.

misconceptions.myth: The same prompt yields the same result with a new model.
misconceptions.fact: Since each model has different default behaviors and supported settings, the instructions and examples must be adjusted accordingly.

misconceptions.myth: Rollback can be done after a problem occurs.
misconceptions.fact: The rollback path must be established before the transition. Otherwise, recovery becomes longer and the damage increases.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The transition consists of three elements: evaluation, gradual deployment, and rollback.
Check model-specific changes before replacement and adjust the prompt accordingly.
Even if passed evaluation, it starts with a portion of traffic to observe customer-specific metrics.
Prepare the rollback path before switching, and add the discovered type to the evaluation set.
closing.reflectionLead: This question is intended to encourage you to think through it on your own. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of the evaluation gate, phased deployment, or rollback is missing from my service's model transition plan?

title: Model migration procedures that reduce regression risk

checks.q: The new model passed the evaluation set criteria, but there were almost no enterprise customer types in the evaluation set that submit long documents. What is the most appropriate transition approach?
options: Since the evaluation has been passed, the entire traffic is converted at once.
The rollback path can be created after the problem occurs.
Same prompt yields same result, so the prompt remains unchanged.
Send only a portion of traffic to the new model first to observe the metrics and pre-define a rollback path.
checks.explain: If the evaluation set fails to capture the actual distribution, passing may still result in regression being hidden. Begin with a subset of traffic, compare against actual environment metrics, and prepare a rollback path to limit damage.

wrong.0: Switching all at once causes problems to spread across all customers.
wrong.1: The rollback path must be established before the transition to avoid prolonging recovery.
wrong.2: Operation behavior and supported settings vary by model; guidelines and examples are adjusted accordingly.
